title_original: BAISHUI’s “A Rainforest of Data” Opens at Fosun Foundation, Shanghai
excerpt_original: Reimagining the ways we see painting through the interplay of data and images. Presented by Fosun Foundation

BAISHUI’s “A Rainforest of Data” Opens at Fosun Foundation, Shanghai

blocks.alt: BAISHUI’s “A Rainforest of Data” Opens at Fosun Foundation, Shanghai

blocks.text: BAISHUI ’s “A Rainforest of Data” at Fosun Foundation, Shanghai, 2026. Courtesy the artist and Fosun Foundation.

From November 11 to December 6, Fosun Foundation presents “A Rainforest of Data,” a solo exhibition by artist BAISHUI in Shanghai. Curated by Cui Cancan, the exhibition spans the first-floor gallery and the fourth-floor outdoor public space, featuring a selection of the artist’s recent works, including seven paintings and the large-scale installation Mirage.

Exploring image generation, data logic, and the language of painting, the exhibition examines how painting redefines its modes of seeing in an era shaped by algorithms, artificial intelligence, and big data.
BAISHUI ’s
Mirage , 2026, 1494 x 1415 x 452 cm, at Fosun Foundation, Shanghai, 2026. Courtesy the artist and Fosun Foundation.

BAISHUI’s creative process typically begins with the use of artificial intelligence, textual prompts, and sketches to generate visual materials and build a personal image library. She then deconstructs, recombines, and refines these materials before moving into the physical process of painting, translating the color relationships of digital images into pigments, brushstrokes, and textures on canvas.

Curator Cui Cancan situates BAISHUI’s practice within the broader historical transformation of image production. In this context, “A Rainforest of Data” refers not only to the densely growing and interwoven images within her paintings, but also to the contemporary visual environment shaped by data and technology. In a rainforest, no individual element exists in isolation; each forms complex relationships with its surroundings. Similarly, BAISHUI’s paintings comprise countless minute elements that overlap and connect to form wholes that cannot be fully grasped at a glance. Viewing the works thus becomes akin to walking through a forest: the eye continually moves into the details before retreating from individual fragments to take in the composition, gradually developing a sense of its entirety.

The title of BAISHUI’s Infinite Dao series takes inspiration from the ancient Chinese philosophical idea that “One gives rise to Two; Two gives rise to Three; Three gives rise to the myriad things.” For BAISHUI, the number three thousand carries a dual significance, serving as both a numerical measure and a philosophical metaphor. In her Infinite Dao series, a single artwork is divided into three thousand parts, which are then reworked and recombined to form an entirely new work. She places her faith in technology’s capacity to bring about fundamental transformations in an age, and believes that artistic innovation should move in tandem with the frontiers of scientific discovery. In close collaboration with AI, she takes her own artistic inspiration and experience as a starting point to generate thousands upon thousands of visual materials, gradually building a personal lexicon and an arsenal of intelligent tools.

As curator observes, “Artistic transformation is a transformation in the mode of production. Perhaps we might put it another way: the art of every age is constituted by an algorithm unique to its time. This is the point of departure for BAISHUI’s practice, and the vision she aspires to realise: to reimagine the algorithm of art itself.”

About the Artist

BAISHUI is a visual and installation artist based in Shanghai and Hong Kong, China. She was recognised in the Western Painting category of Forbes China’s 2025 selection of leading contemporary artists.

BAISHUI’s artistic practice is grounded in a highly original creative system with a clearly defined methodology. Through long-term interdisciplinary research, she has independently developed a working approach known as “Flow”, centred on perceptual impulses, structural thinking, and deep collaboration with artificial intelligence. A defining feature of this method is the integration of online digital generation and offline physical production into a unified creative system, establishing an ongoing, reciprocal relationship in which the two processes continuously inform and shape one another, rather than following a conventional sequence of translation from one medium to another.

Through “Flow”, BAISHUI brings artificial intelligence, material systems, and the artist’s own judgement into a shared generative structure. Creation thus becomes less a matter of controlling a single medium or predetermined outcome than a process of continuous recalibration amid uncertainty. Within this framework of collaboration, digital generation and physical production mutually shape one another. This approach not only reconfigures the relationship between image generation and material production, but also offers a practice-based model for the application of artificial intelligence in contemporary art, one centred on thinking, structure, and perception, while expanding the possibilities of artistic creation in an age of technology.
